title: Functional Programming Basics
learningObjectives: Explain the main paradigm or design technique.
Identify how behavior and responsibilities are organized.
Trace the provided examples and predict results.
Describe an advantage and a trade-off.
Apply the technique to a small design scenario.

understand.concept: Functional programming emphasizes functions and transformations, reducing unintended state changes and side effects. Common ideas include pure functions, immutable data, function composition, and higher-order functions. Languages differ in how strongly they support or enforce these practices; functional style can be used within multi-paradigm languages.
understand.whyItMatters: Functional techniques make transformations easier to reason about, test, and reuse. Avoiding mutation can reduce bugs, though copying data or using a purely functional design may require different trade-offs and learning effort.
understand.analogy: A recipe that transforms ingredients without changing the original batch illustrates a transformation, though software functions can have side effects.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; language features, contracts, and runtime behavior vary.

explain.narrative: Trace each example and identify the contract or style it demonstrates. Consider how a caller depends on the behavior, what could change, and where the approach might become rigid or unclear. Paradigms are design tools; avoid forcing a style when a simpler structure is more readable.

examples.title: Pure function
examples.explanation: Same input produces the same result and does not change external state.

examples.title: Map transformation
examples.explanation: Map transforms each element into a result sequence.

examples.title: Filter
examples.explanation: Filter keeps values matching a predicate.

examples.title: Composition
examples.explanation: Functions are composed by passing one result into another.

examples.title: Avoid hidden mutation
examples.explanation: A new array is created rather than mutating the original.

commonMistakes: Using inheritance only to share code without a meaningful relationship.
Assuming an interface guarantees correct behavior by itself.
Treating imperative and declarative approaches as mutually exclusive.

guidedTask.title: Guided practice: Functional Programming Basics
guidedTask.instructions: Study a small program and identify how this paradigm or design approach is applied.
steps: State the problem the code solves.
Identify its types, functions, components, or style.
Trace the behavior and any data changes.
Describe one strength and one limitation.
Suggest a simpler or alternative design when appropriate.
guidedTask.starterCode: // Create a small example that demonstrates this approach.

independentTask.title: Independent practice: apply this design approach
independentTask.instructions: Create a small program or refactor a simple example to demonstrate the technique.
requirements: Describe the task and intended behavior.
Include at least two operations or components.
Explain the design relationship or style.
Add a sample output or test.

hints: Keep the design focused on the problem.
Prefer clear contracts and small responsibilities.
Consider mixing styles when it improves clarity.

questions.prompt: What is the common difference between inheritance and composition?
options: Inheritance derives from another type; composition combines parts or capabilities
questions.answer: Inheritance derives from another type; composition combines parts or capabilities
questions.explanation: Inheritance specializes a parent type; composition assembles separate components.
